articles.title: Middleton pupils form giant star to celebrate Rhodes Green school's new name
articles.excerpt: The former Little Heaton primary school welcomed the Bishop of Middleton for a celebration of its new name, with classroom visits, worship and a tree planting.
articles.content_html:
Pupils at a Middleton primary school formed a giant star in their playground to celebrate its new name during a visit from the Bishop of Middleton.

Rhodes Green Church of England Primary School, on Boardman Lane in Rhodes, welcomed the Rt Revd Mark Davies on Thursday 5 November. Children, staff, parents and members of the community joined the celebrations, which included classroom visits, worship and the planting of a commemorative tree.

The school was previously known as Little Heaton CE Primary School. It changed its name in September to reflect its connection with the Rhodes community, where many of its pupils live. Rochdale Council's school directory also records the change.

The playground photograph brought the school's Christian vision, “Shine as stars in the world”, into view, with children lining up to form the outline of a star.

Headteacher Chloe Noon said: “Rhodes Green is about much more than a new name. It's about the school we're building together and making sure every child feels happy, safe and proud to belong here.”

She added: “We want our children to have big dreams, to believe in themselves and to know that they can achieve wonderful things. Seeing them come together today, and hearing Bishop Mark share that same message, has been really special for all of us.”

The head boy and head girl showed the Bishop around the school, taking him into classrooms to meet children from every year group before an assembly with families. Pupils and staff gave readings during the celebration.

Bishop Mark, who has known the school for more than 20 years, said: “Today has been absolutely amazing and such a tremendous joy and a great blessing. Today represents a new and exciting chapter. A name says so much and is so, so important.”

During a conversation with pupil leaders, he spoke about teachers and church leaders who had encouraged him and urged the children to believe in their own ambitions.

Cranmer Education Trust, which supplied the account of the visit, said the school joined the trust in 2024. Its chief executive Julie Hollis and chair of trustees Janet Gregory attended, alongside the Rev'd Jenni Beaumont from All Saints, Rhodes.

For families who know the school by its former name, Rhodes Green is the same Boardman Lane school. Its current information is available at https://www.rhodesgreen-primary.org/.

articles.title: Greater Manchester Police to host pop-up events to combat online scams in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: In a bid to protect shoppers from online fraud, Greater Manchester Police will hold pop-up events in Rochdale next week, providing essential advice and support.
articles.content_html:
In the lead-up to Christmas, Greater Manchester Police (GMP) is organising pop-up fraud-prevention events in Rochdale to help shoppers avoid online scams.

The sessions will take place at Virgin Money on Yorkshire Street on Tuesday, November 10, and at Halifax on the same street on Wednesday, November 11, both from 10am to 1pm.

The events are being hosted by GMP’s Economic Crime Unit, which aims to educate the public about the various types of scams, from simple confidence tricks to sophisticated online fraud.

Attendees will have the opportunity to speak with police staff and volunteers about any concerns they may have regarding fraud and cyber crime.

GMP has emphasised the importance of staying informed about the latest scams and has provided tips to reduce the risk of becoming a victim.

These include never sharing passwords or personal details, regularly updating devices and apps, and ensuring that emails and attachments are only opened if they come from trusted sources.

These pop-up events are crucial as they provide direct access to expert advice and support for local residents, particularly during the busy shopping season. By attending, shoppers can better protect themselves from potential scams and ensure a safer festive period.

articles.title: New Ukrainian GCSE welcomed for Rochdale pupils
articles.excerpt: Rochdale MP Paul Waugh has welcomed plans for a Ukrainian GCSE, with teaching expected from September 2028 and first exams in 2029.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale pupils are set to have the opportunity to study for a new Ukrainian GCSE, with teaching expected to begin in September 2028 and the first exams planned for summer 2029.

Rochdale MP Paul Waugh welcomed the announcement, saying it would give children who fled Russia’s war the chance to gain a qualification in Ukrainian.

In a statement shared alongside a photograph of a group holding a Ukrainian flag, Mr Waugh said Ukrainian child refugees in the UK had been told to study Russian at GCSE as an alternative to Ukrainian. He described that situation as unacceptable for children who had fled the war.

“I'm so proud to have such a brilliant Ukrainian community in Rochdale, and I'm glad to have helped make this possible for them,” he said.

The qualification will be developed by AQA and will be open to all pupils, giving young Ukrainians a way to gain recognition for their language skills and maintain a connection to their heritage.

It is expected to be available in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Like other modern foreign language GCSEs, it will assess listening, speaking, reading and writing, alongside the cultural and historical context of the language.

The timetable remains subject to Ofqual approval. The national announcement does not yet set out which individual Rochdale schools will offer the course.

For families in Rochdale’s Ukrainian community, the planned qualification offers a future route to formal recognition of a language that is an important part of their identity.

articles.title: Cronkeyshaw Common bonfire night proves a huge success as quiet fireworks light up the sky
articles.excerpt: Quiet fireworks set to music including Queen’s Don’t Stop Me Now have delighted the crowd at Cronkeyshaw Common, with little to no traffic disruption reported so far.
articles.content_html:
Cronkeyshaw Common’s bonfire night has so far proved a huge success, with a colourful fireworks display set to music and little to no traffic disruption reported around the event.

An eyewitness report to Rochdale Daily described an evening enjoyed by those watching, with “quiet” fireworks lighting up the sky to a soundtrack including Queen’s Don’t Stop Me Now.

The reduced-noise display was intended to help limit distress to wildlife and people who find loud fireworks difficult, while keeping the spectacle and shared enjoyment of bonfire night.

The photograph accompanying this update captures the crowd watching bright trails and bursts of colour above the common in Syke.

Despite temporary road closures and parking restrictions around the site, the report from the evening so far is of little to no traffic disruption. That is an observation from the event, rather than a borough-wide traffic assessment.

The free event on Wednesday 4 November was organised by Rochdale Borough Council, following this week’s displays in Middleton and Heywood. The advertised programme ran from 6pm to 10pm, with the bonfire scheduled for 7pm and the reduced-noise fireworks set to music for 7.30pm.

Road closures and parking restrictions were scheduled from 4pm to 9pm around Greenbank Road, Dewhirst Road, Fieldhouse Road, Joy Street and Binns Nook Road, with additional waiting restrictions on nearby streets.

There is no parking on the common. Visitors are asked to remain considerate of residents and keep access clear as they leave.

articles.title: Former non-league footballer James Moore builds multi-million pound shop empire
articles.excerpt: James Moore, a former non-league footballer, has established a successful retail business, Mintro, with eight stores across the North West, including Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
James Moore, a former non-league footballer, has transitioned from the pitch to the retail world, building a multi-million pound business empire with his company Mintro.

The 38-year-old, who played for clubs including Bury FC and Glossop North End, now operates eight stores across the North West, including one in Rochdale.

Moore's journey began at the age of 18 when he took a Saturday job at BrightHouse in Hyde.

His success in retail led him to manage various stores, eventually taking on a Cash Generator shop in Rochdale in 2017, which he transformed into his own brand, Mintro.

The store focuses on buying and selling pre-owned technology, jewellery, and designer items without the pawn shop model of loans and interest.

Despite the challenges posed by the Covid pandemic, which temporarily closed his stores, Moore leveraged the situation to secure financing for expansion.

His business now generates around £5 million annually, with plans to grow further, including a recent sponsorship deal with Stockport County FC, a team he once played against as a child.

Moore's story showcases resilience and adaptability, demonstrating how skills from sports can translate into business success. His journey serves as an inspiration for local entrepreneurs and highlights the potential for growth in the retail sector, particularly in Rochdale.

articles.title: Rochdale Asda worker's kindness a 'breath of fresh air' for widowed customer
articles.excerpt: Shaheda times her help around an older customer's shopping trips after the woman lost her husband, scanning and packing her shopping and stopping for a chat.
articles.content_html:
A worker at Asda's Rochdale store has been praised for looking out for an older customer after the woman was widowed.

Shaheda first noticed something had changed when the customer, who used to shop with her husband, stopped coming in for a while. When she next saw her, the woman was shopping with her daughter, and the pair told her what had happened.

The daughter lives in London and was worried about how her mother would cope on her own. Shaheda promised to look after her and told her which days she works, so the customer could time her visits for when Shaheda would be there.

Now, when the customer comes in, Shaheda scans and packs her shopping, fetches her a chair and makes time for a chat.

The customer told the store's customer manager, Dave, how much the help meant to her. Dave said: "The lady told me that ever since she lost her husband three months ago, Shaheda has been like a breath of fresh air in her life every time she shops – not just because of the help she offers, but as an emotional support and somebody to chat to."

Shaheda said: "I used to see the lady come in with her husband all the time and then didn't see her for a while. Then I saw her shopping with her daughter, and they told me what had happened. I told her to come and see me every time she came in... and she does. We have a good chat and I help her, as she does struggle a bit."

She added: "She thanks me every single time and I go, 'no, you don't need to thank me'. It's sweet, though. I like to think that somebody would do that for my own mum. I always think too that one day I could be in that position. It doesn't cost anything to be pleasant and kind, does it?"

For someone adjusting to life alone after a bereavement, a familiar face on a weekly errand can make a real difference, and the help Shaheda gives costs nothing but a little time.

articles.title: Rochdale's pathology teams support millions of tests during National Pathology Week
articles.excerpt: As National Pathology Week is celebrated, Rochdale's pathology teams highlight their vital role in healthcare, processing over 10 million samples annually.
articles.content_html:
This week marks National Pathology Week, a time to recognise the essential work of pathology teams across Greater Manchester, including those in Rochdale.

These teams process more than 10 million samples and conduct over 35 million tests each year, playing a crucial role in patient care.

Pathology services are integral to approximately 95% of clinical pathways, providing the diagnostic information that clinicians rely on to diagnose illnesses, guide treatments, and monitor ongoing care. Despite their critical role, many patients may never meet the professionals working behind the scenes in pathology laboratories.

The Northern Care Alliance's pathology workforce includes nearly 700 staff members across various locations, including Rochdale, Oldham, Salford, and Bury. This diverse team comprises biomedical scientists, pathologists, clinical scientists, and other specialists who work together to ensure efficient and accurate testing.

Recent advancements in technology, such as the introduction of automated biopsy processing in Oldham, have improved workflow and increased capacity, allowing biomedical scientists to focus more on specialised diagnostic work.

As the healthcare landscape evolves, the importance of pathology services in supporting patient care continues to grow. The implementation of a new Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) has also transformed how laboratories manage samples and results, ensuring uninterrupted services for patients.

In fact, around 95% of clinical pathways rely on pathology services, providing the diagnostic information clinicians need to diagnose illness, guide treatment and monitor ongoing care. Alex, biomedical scientist in the Royal Oldham lab At the heart of this work colleagues are combining scientific expertise with the latest technology to deliver faster, more efficient testing for patients. Earlier this year, the Oldham laboratory introduced new automated biopsy processing technology designed to support specimen preparation around the clock. The system can operate 24 hours a day, seven days a week, helping improve workflow, create additional capacity and enable biomedical scientists to spend more time on highly specialised diagnostic work. The introduction of the technology builds on a wider programme of innovation within the laboratory, which has also led the way in adopting digital pathology, allowing specialists to review biopsy samples digitally and collaborate more easily across healthcare organisations. The past year has also seen colleagues successfully implement a new Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) across pathology services. The major programme has transformed how laboratories manage samples and results, with teams across all sites working together to ensure services for patients continued uninterrupted throughout the transition. The NCA's pathology workforce includes almost 700 colleagues working across Oldham, Salford, Rochdale, Bury, Wigan, Wrightington and Leigh. Together they represent a diverse range of professions including biomedical scientists, pathologists, clinical scientists, mortuary practitioners, biomedical support workers, transfusion practitioners, microbiologists, virologists, biochemists, point of care testing teams, administrators, porters and messengers. Every day, these teams support services spanning laboratory medicine, microbiology, cellular pathology, mortuary services, blood sciences and point of care testing. David Muskett, lead biomedical scientist at the Northern Care Alliance, said: “Everything we do is focused on helping clinicians get the accurate diagnostic information they need as quickly as possible. We know that behind every sample is a patient waiting for answers, and every improvement we make helps reduce delays, supports faster decision-making and, ultimately, means patients spend less time anxiously waiting for test results." “This year has seen significant change and I am incredibly proud of how our teams have embraced these developments while continuing to deliver high-quality services for patients.” Pathology colleagues at Royal Oldham. articles.title: Investigation works begin at former Turner Brothers factory site in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Spodden Park Ltd has started investigations to locate buried asbestos at the derelict Turner Brothers factory, aiming for future redevelopment.
articles.content_html:
Spodden Park Ltd has commenced investigation works at the former Turner Brothers factory site in Spotland, Rochdale, to locate buried asbestos.

This site, once the world’s largest producer of asbestos, has been a concern for local residents due to the toxic materials associated with its history.

The investigations will be carried out by a specialist contractor over the coming weeks. Spodden Park Ltd assures that no asbestos will be disturbed during this phase, which aims to inform a safe remediation strategy for the site.

Heavy machinery will be used, but the company has stated that no buildings will be demolished during this process.

Locals have recently observed workers in overalls and diggers at the site, which has been nicknamed 'Rochdale's Chernobyl' due to its hazardous past.

The landowner has also issued warnings against trespassing, highlighting the dangers posed by the ongoing works and the need for enhanced security measures to prevent unauthorized access.

While the future plans for the site have not been fully disclosed, it is understood that Spodden Park Ltd intends to redevelop the area, potentially including housing and a park.

This follows a previous proposal for 650 homes in the early 2000s, which has since been scaled back.

articles.title: Middleton residents warned about scammers posing as council officials
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has issued a warning to residents in Middleton about scammers posing as council officials to gain entry into homes.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Middleton are being warned about scammers posing as council officials in an attempt to gain entry into their homes. This warning follows reports of several incidents in the area, prompting Rochdale Council to take action.

The council stated, "We have been made aware of bogus cold callers posing as council officers to gain entry into homes." They emphasised that all legitimate council staff carry identification and can produce it upon request.

Residents are advised to check for ID before allowing anyone into their homes.

If residents are unsure about a caller's identity or if they cannot produce an official badge, they are encouraged to refuse entry.

The council also reminded residents that services and appointments can only be booked and paid for in advance through their contact centre at 01706 647474.

Residents who have experienced similar visits are urged to report them to Greater Manchester Police, either online or by calling 101. This warning is crucial for ensuring the safety and security of residents in the community.

If you’re unsure if the person is a legitimate caller, call their head office using the number from a recent bill, email or website. The goods and services offered by rogue traders can range from prize draws to psychic letters. Do not give out personal details or bank information unless absolutely necessary. Warning signs that a salesperson isn’t legitimate include pressuring you to make a purchase or responding to the offer straight away. If you are asked to make a purchase to win a prize or call a premium rate number to claim an offer, it is likely to be a scam. A salesperson not wanting to give their address or contact details, or asking for your bank details are other red flags. If you pay or agree to pay over £42 for any goods or services on the doorstep, you have 14 days to cancel the agreement without penalty and be fully refunded. articles.title: Zambrero to give away free burritos at new Mellor Street restaurant in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Zambrero will hand out hundreds of free burritos and bowls from 11am to 2pm on Thursday 12 November to mark its new Mellor Street restaurant, which opened in September.
articles.content_html:
Zambrero is giving away free burritos and bowls at its new Mellor Street restaurant in Rochdale next week, as a thank-you to the town six weeks after it opened.

The Free Burrito Day takes place on Thursday 12 November, from 11am to 2pm. The company says it will hand out hundreds of freshly made burritos and bowls during the three-hour window, and is advising people to arrive early to avoid the queues. Zambrero's resident scratch DJ, NC, will be playing hip hop and crowd favourites throughout.

The restaurant opened on 25 September and is Zambrero's first site in Rochdale. It offers dine-in, takeaway and delivery, has seating for 18, and is close to the town centre and local colleges. According to the company, the opening has created six jobs.

The menu centres on burritos and bowls, alongside tacos, nachos and quesadillas, made to order at the counter. Customers can choose from slow-cooked fillings, salad, rice, beans and toppings, and there are vegetarian, vegan and halal options.

The site also brings the chain's Plate 4 Plate scheme to Rochdale, under which a meal is donated to someone in need for every burrito or bowl bought. Zambrero says the scheme has provided more than 110 million meals worldwide.

Damian Bennett, Zambrero's development agent for Greater Manchester and West Yorkshire, said: "We've had a fantastic response since opening our doors in Rochdale and this Free Burrito Day is our way of thanking the local community for its support. We can't wait to welcome residents, students and local workers to come along, enjoy a free burrito or bowl and experience what Zambrero is all about."

He added that every burrito and bowl given away on the day, and bought afterwards, would count towards the Plate 4 Plate programme.

Rochdale is Zambrero's 18th UK opening since the brand arrived in Britain in 2021, with other sites in London, Manchester, Birmingham, Reading, Essex, Basingstoke, Northampton and Glasgow. The company was founded in Australia in 2005 and now has more than 350 locations worldwide.

For town-centre businesses, a new food outlet within reach of the colleges adds to the lunchtime trade around Mellor Street. Have you tried it yet, and what other food or shops would you like to see open in the town centre? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title: Resident escapes fire at Lonsdale Court sheltered housing in Middleton
articles.excerpt: A resident self-rescued from a fire at Lonsdale Court in Middleton, prompting a swift response from fire crews and support services.
articles.content_html:
A fire broke out in a second-floor flat at Lonsdale Court, a sheltered housing residence in Middleton, on the evening of November 5. Fire crews from Chadderton, Blackley, and Heywood fire stations responded quickly to the incident, which was reported just before 7pm.

Eyewitnesses reported seeing multiple fire engines and police vehicles on Sedgley Street and Nelson Street as the emergency services arrived. One resident managed to escape the flat before firefighters arrived and was assessed at the scene by North West Ambulance Service (NWAS).

The fire service confirmed that all residents in the neighbouring flats were evacuated safely and are being supported by Rochdale Homes. Following the extinguishing of the fire, safety checks were conducted to ensure the building was secure for re-entry.

This incident underscores the importance of fire safety measures in residential settings, particularly for vulnerable populations such as the elderly. Residents are reminded to ensure their smoke alarms are functioning and to have an escape plan in place.

articles.title: Rochdale Council warns families of confirmed measles cases
articles.excerpt: Families in Rochdale are urged to be vigilant for measles symptoms following confirmed cases, with health officials advising vaccinations.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has issued a warning to families after confirmed cases of measles were reported in the borough. The council highlighted that some of these cases have resulted in visits to Accident and Emergency departments, raising concerns about the potential spread of the virus.

Health officials are advising residents to be aware of the symptoms of measles, which include high fever, runny nose, cough, red and watery eyes, Koplik spots, and a rash that typically starts on the face and spreads across the body.

Measles can lead to serious health complications, particularly for vulnerable individuals such as infants and those with weakened immune systems.

The council has urged parents to ensure their children are vaccinated with the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine, which is usually administered at 12 and 18 months of age.

Those who have not yet received the vaccine are encouraged to contact their GP to arrange an appointment.

This warning serves as a crucial reminder for families in Rochdale about the importance of recognising measles symptoms and ensuring vaccinations are up to date. Vaccination can help prevent the spread of this highly contagious disease.

articles.title: Rochdale achieves 21 gold awards at North West in Bloom
articles.excerpt: Rochdale has celebrated a successful year at the North West in Bloom awards, achieving 21 gold awards and multiple category wins, including Best Town Centre.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale has celebrated a remarkable achievement at the North West in Bloom awards, securing 21 gold awards and eight overall category wins.

The results were announced during the annual ceremony held at Toughsheet Community Stadium in Bolton on 30 October 2026, following visits from Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) judges over the summer.

The awards highlight the borough's commitment to horticulture, environmental responsibility, and community participation. Rochdale town centre's horticulturists continued their winning streak, taking gold and the title of Best Town Centre, alongside their success at the recent RHS Britain in Bloom awards.

Phil Massey, treasurer of Rochdale in Bloom, received an outstanding contribution award for his significant efforts in supporting the borough's success.

The Baillie Street Quarter won the new Best Art in the Community award for its artwork from the Common Walls International Mural Festival, led by local artist Hayley Garner.

Other notable winners included the Hampton by Hilton hotel, which won gold in its category, and Heywood town centre, which also achieved gold thanks to the efforts of local volunteers.

The success of Rochdale in Bloom not only showcases the borough's beauty but also fosters community pride and environmental awareness.

articles.title: Rochdale Council leaves door open for Hopwood Hall reconciliation after court ruling
articles.excerpt: Following a recent High Court ruling, Rochdale Council has expressed willingness to engage with filmmaker Hopwood DePree regarding the future of Hopwood Hall, which has been a point of contention since the termination of their agreement in 2024.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has indicated a willingness to engage in discussions with filmmaker Hopwood DePree regarding the future of Hopwood Hall, following a recent High Court ruling that upheld the council's decision to terminate their agreement.

This development comes after a two-day trial at Manchester Civil Justice Centre in September, where the court ruled that the council acted lawfully in ending the exclusivity agreement with DePree, who had sought to purchase the historic site for £1.

The council's option agreement with DePree, which began in 2017, was terminated in October 2024, leading to a legal dispute. DePree, who claims ancestral ties to the hall, believed he had a binding agreement to purchase the property.

However, the court found that a planning approval granted in 2022 did not trigger the option to buy the hall for the nominal fee.

In response to the court's decision, DePree has issued an open letter to the council, outlining his terms for a potential resolution.

He expressed a desire for constructive dialogue and transparency regarding the council's decisions, including a request for the release of documents related to the handling of the hall's management. DePree has suggested that an independent review could help clarify the situation and facilitate discussions.

Council leader Neil Emmott reiterated that the council's 'door is always open' for DePree to present a viable plan for Hopwood Hall's future.

Both parties have acknowledged that the costly court battle could have been avoided, and there is hope for an amicable resolution that benefits the community and preserves the historic site.

Since then, Mr DePree, who claims ancestral connections with the 1400s stately home, has felt he had a legally binding agreement to purchase Hopwood Hall for £1. ‌ However, in September, following a two-day trial in Manchester Civil Justice Centre, the court ruled that the council was not acting unlawfully when it ended the exclusivity agreement with the American filmmaker. ‌ To get the very latest from Manchester's political scene in your newsfeed - click here to add the MEN as your preferred Google source The High Court found that the ‘change of use’ planning approval granted in 2022 wasn’t enough to trigger the option to purchase the hall for a ‘peppercorn fee’ – £1. Therefore, Mr DePree’s claim was lost. Now, the filmmaker has issued an open letter to town hall bosses to set out his terms for a resolution discussion. This comes after council leader Neil Emmott told the latest town hall meeting his ‘door is always open’ to Mr DePree. ‌ He added that if Mr DePree came back with a viable plan for the future of Hopwood Hall, the council would listen. View 4 Images Hopwood Depree is one of the descendants of the family who founded the hall (Image: Manchester Evening News) ‌ Both sides have said a costly court battle could have been avoided. But Mr DePree’s latest open letter to the local authority suggested it was the council that took ‘an incredibly aggressive legal route of termination and locking them out of Hopwood Hall’. The council has always maintained that the volunteer group was barred due to safety reasons. The reasons for the ending of the agreement by the council and being booted out of the hall are still something Mr DePree says he doesn’t understand. ‌ The US-born adopted Middletonian wants to see the council release documents about communications between authorities about how they handled dealings about the hall; commission an independent review; correct inaccurate public statements about his community-led effort; and to pause further action in the ongoing legal proceedings and enter into discussions to find an amicable solution. What the letter says In his letter, he said: “I hope we can find an amicable resolution for Hopwood Hall. At the October 15, 2026 public council meeting, you stated that your ‘door is always open’ and ‘Rochdale council is willing to listen’ if I come forward with a sustainable plan, following the council’s unexpected termination of our community-led rescue in 2024. ‌ View 4 Images An aerial view shows Hopwood Hall, the ancestral home of US film producer Hopwood DePree, that dates from the 15th century, which he is in the process of restoring, in Middleton, northern England on November 28, 2022. - As a child, Hopwood DePree had heard family stories about owning a castle in England but never took them too seriously. That was until he tracked down the 15th century castle with 16 rooms in the countryside near Manchester. In 2017 the American quit California to work full-time on restoring the building -- a task that keeps him very busy. - TO GO WITH AFP STORY BY Caroline TAIX (Photo by OLI SCARFF / AFP) / TO GO WITH AFP STORY BY Caroline TAIX (Photo by OLI SCARFF/AFP via Getty Images) “I would welcome constructive discussions but they must begin with a clear explanation of why our previous proposal was rejected. Nearly two years after our heritage team was locked out, the council still has not provided meaningful answers and continues to refuse to release documents and communications about decisions taken. ‌ “Despite our challenges, I remain open to constructive dialogue, including an independently moderated public forum where councillors, volunteers and residents can address concerns and explore Hopwood Hall’s future. “Given the time-sensitive nature of our legal options, we must reserve our rights. However, this should not prevent prompt, productive discussion aimed at reaching a resolution without further litigation. My hope is that sums that will otherwise be expended on legal costs can be better used for the benefit of the Hall. ‌ “My commitment remains to see Hopwood Hall rescued, restored and enjoyed by future generations. I hope you will respond openly to these requests.” Currently, Mr DePree’s legal team has another two weeks to decide if they want to appeal the High Court decision made in September. ‌ What the council and its leader has said A council spokesperson said: “The council successfully defended the High Court claim concerning Hopwood Hall and, as the period in which the claimant may seek permission to appeal has not yet expired, it would not be appropriate to comment further on the proceedings or the issues raised in the open letter at this stage. “We remain focused on securing a sustainable future for Hopwood Hall, once the legal process has concluded.” ‌ After being quizzed on the next steps for Hopwood Hall previously, Coun Emmott did not clarify a specific use for its future, but vowed to bring it back into use for the wider community. At the latest town hall meeting, Coun Emmott said: “The High Court’s judgment in relation to Hopwood Hall does not necessarily mark the end of the legal process. ‌ “Mr DePree has the right to seek permission to appeal the decision. The court has directed that any application for permission to appeal must be lodged by November 18, 2026, although there is scope for this deadline to be extended to November 28, 2026. View 4 Images Rochdale council leader, Neil Emmott (Image: Kenny Brown | Manchester Evening News) ‌ “The council was awarded total costs of £114,000. I can confirm these monies will be reinvested into the project. As part of any appeal process, Mr DePree would be required to make a payment into court of approximately £80,000 towards Rochdale council’s legal costs. “Should Mr DePree pursue an appeal, he would first need to obtain the court’s permission to proceed. This would require him to demonstrate that the proposed appeal has a real prospect of success or that there is another compelling reason for it to be heard. ‌ “Only Mr DePree and his legal advisers can determine whether an appeal is pursued. It is understandable that emotions remain strong within the local community, particularly among those volunteers who have dedicated considerable time and effort to the Hopwood Hall project. However, the council cannot move forward until the matter of the appeal is settled. “I can, though, assure the council and the people of Middleton that we remain focussed on the future of Hopwood Hall and the opportunities that now exist to secure its long-term restoration and preservation. More than £1.6m has already been spent on repairs to the hall by the council and Historic England. We will continue to invest in vital repairs to this historic building. articles.title: Eighth arrest in property damage investigation covering Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Police have received 63 reports of damage to HMOs or properties mistaken for them across six Greater Manchester districts, including Rochdale. Eight arrests have been made and one person has been brought before court.
articles.content_html:
Police have received 63 reports of damage to properties across six Greater Manchester districts, including Rochdale, in an investigation that has led to eight arrests.

In an update issued on Friday 6 November, Greater Manchester Police said one person had been brought before the courts. The release did not identify that person or give details of the case.

The investigation concerns houses in multiple occupation, known as HMOs, and properties mistaken for HMOs. Reports have been received from Rochdale, Salford, Tameside, Stockport, Bolton and Wigan since the start of October.

The figure of 63 covers all six districts. Police have not given a separate Rochdale total or identified the properties affected in the borough.

The most recent arrest was made on Monday 2 November. In its earlier announcement, GMP said a 29-year-old man had been arrested that morning on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage. The force did not state where that arrest took place.

Chief Superintendent Marcus Noden said officers had been working with partner organisations across Greater Manchester to understand the damage and respond.

He said: “Our investigation has led to eight people being brought into our custody so far and, since making the latest arrest, we've seen three further reports of similar damage.”

He added: “You will continue to see our officers in areas that have been affected by this criminality as we continue our enforcement action.”

Police are continuing to appeal for information. Anyone who can help can call 101 or report information online at https://www.gmp.police.uk/.

Information can also be passed anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

No finding of guilt should be inferred from an arrest or court appearance. Anyone accused is presumed innocent unless and until convicted.

Updated on 6 November 2026 with GMP's latest total of 63 reports, confirmation that one person has been brought before court and the continuing appeal. The number of arrests remains eight. This article was first published on 2 November.

articles.title: Moor Road roadworks in Littleborough set to begin on 5 November 2026
articles.excerpt: Roadworks on Moor Road in Littleborough will start on 5 November 2026, affecting local traffic for up to 21 days.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks on Moor Road in Littleborough will commence on 5 November 2026. The work is expected to last for a maximum of 21 days, concluding by 26 November 2026, or sooner if repairs are completed ahead of schedule.

The roadworks will result in a temporary closure of part of Moor Road, specifically from 104 metres north of the junction with Temple Kane to 10 metres further up the road. This closure will affect traffic flow, particularly for residents and commuters in the area.

Local roads including Calderbrook Road, Barnes Meadows, and Temple Lane may experience increased traffic as drivers seek alternative routes during the closure. Residents should plan their journeys accordingly and allow extra time for travel.

For more information on the roadworks and to view a map of the affected area, residents can visit the Rochdale Borough Council website.

articles.content_html:

Henderson has been a key player for Rochdale since joining the club, contributing significantly with over 100 goals. His dedication has made him a fan favourite and a respected figure in the club's history.

The match will take place at the Crown Oil Arena, where fans are expected to celebrate Henderson's achievement. His record-breaking appearance highlights his commitment to the club over nearly a decade.

Fans are encouraged to attend the match to support Henderson and witness this historic moment.

articles.content_html:

The proposed redevelopment will involve a complete knock-down of the existing structure, followed by the construction of a new forecourt. This project is expected to enhance the overall customer experience at the site.

This redevelopment reflects a broader trend in the fuel retail sector, where companies are investing in modern facilities to meet changing consumer demands. As the project progresses, updates will be provided to keep the community informed.

articles.excerpt: The Ignite Fire Festival, organised by the Rochdale Development Agency, will showcase a new multi-sensory experience called Body, focusing on human metabolism.
articles.content_html:
The Ignite Fire Festival is set to take place in Rochdale, featuring a unique multi-sensory experience called Body. Organised by the Rochdale Development Agency, this festival will mark its north-west premiere, providing an engaging educational experience about human metabolism.

Scheduled as part of the countdown to Christmas, the festival will introduce dazzling new trails and attractions, promising to captivate audiences of all ages. The event aims to blend entertainment with education, making it a significant addition to Rochdale's festive calendar.

The Ignite Fire Festival will take place on November 25, 2026, at various locations throughout Rochdale. Attendees can expect a vibrant atmosphere filled with light, sound, and interactive installations designed to enhance their understanding of the human body.

This festival not only aims to entertain but also to educate the community about health and wellness, making it a valuable event for local families and visitors alike.

As the festival approaches, residents are encouraged to participate and enjoy the festive spirit it brings to the town.

articles.title: Three-year-old boy remains critical in hospital after incident at Middleton nursery
articles.excerpt: A three-year-old boy is in critical condition following a medical emergency at Cosy Toes nursery in Middleton, with police confirming the incident is not suspicious.
articles.content_html:
A three-year-old boy is currently in critical condition in hospital following a medical emergency at Cosy Toes nursery in Middleton. Emergency services were called to the nursery on Mainway East on Monday afternoon, November 2, after reports of the incident.

The response involved three police vehicles, an ambulance, and a rapid response paramedic car, with an air ambulance also landing nearby. A spokesperson for Greater Manchester Police confirmed that the incident is not being treated as suspicious and that inquiries are ongoing.

Cosy Toes nursery, which is part of a chain operating four nurseries across Middleton, provides daycare for children up to five years old. The nursery has been approached for further information regarding the incident, but no additional details have been released.

As the boy continues to fight for his life in hospital, the community is left concerned about his wellbeing and the circumstances surrounding the emergency. Updates from authorities will be crucial for those affected and the wider community.

articles.title: Rochdale resident seeks planning permission for new garden wall and fencing
articles.excerpt: Lewis Mahoney has applied for retrospective planning permission for a new garden wall and fencing at his home in Rochdale, which has raised concerns among local planners.
articles.content_html:
Lewis Mahoney has applied for retrospective planning permission for a new garden wall and fencing at his property located at 1 Bates Close, Rochdale.

The application has sparked discussions among local planners regarding the impact of the new structure on the character of the surrounding area.

Planners have expressed concerns that the new fencing is out of character with the existing street scene, which typically features low-rise fencing and lacks hard boundary treatments.

This has led to a debate about how the new installation fits within the established aesthetic of Bates Close.

The planning committee is currently reviewing the application and considering the implications of the new wall and fencing on the neighbourhood's visual coherence.

The outcome of this review will determine whether the retrospective permission will be granted or if the structure will need to be modified or removed.

This case highlights the ongoing challenges residents face when making changes to their properties in ways that may not align with local planning guidelines. The decision will be significant for Mahoney and could set a precedent for similar applications in the area.

articles.title: Asda worker Saheda Bibi praised for supporting widowed customer in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Saheda Bibi, an Asda employee in Rochdale, has been recognised for her kindness in helping a recently widowed customer with her shopping needs.
articles.content_html:
An Asda employee in Rochdale has received praise for her compassionate support of a recently widowed customer. Saheda Bibi, 43, has worked at the store since 2012 and made a promise to look after the woman after learning about her loss.

The customer’s daughter, who lives in London, expressed concern about how her mother would manage alone following her husband's death. Saheda reassured her by sharing her work schedule, allowing the daughter to plan her mother's shopping trips accordingly.

Since then, Saheda has assisted the woman with her shopping, ensuring she has a chair to sit on and taking the time to chat with her.

The customer was so grateful for Saheda's kindness that she contacted the store's customer manager, Dave Jeffs, to express her appreciation.

In recognition of her outstanding service, Dave has nominated Saheda for an Asda Service Superstar Award, highlighting the positive impact she has made on the customer's life during a difficult time.

articles.excerpt: Police seized six vehicles, including an e-scooter, during a road safety operation in Rochdale, with multiple drivers reported for various offences.

Police seized six vehicles during a road safety operation in Rochdale on November 4, 2026. The operation involved officers from the Rochdale North and Rochdale East neighbourhood policing teams, alongside Greater Manchester Police’s traffic division and Rochdale Council’s Licensing and Trading Standards teams.

A total of 104 vehicles were stopped during the operation. Among the seized vehicles was an e-scooter.

One driver was arrested on suspicion of drug-driving, while 11 others were reported for having illegal number plates. Additional reports included one driver for not wearing a seat belt, another for driving without a licence, and two motorists for driving without insurance.

The operation aimed to enhance road safety in the area, with GMP Rochdale noting that while many drivers and vehicles were operating within the law, a small number were not. This initiative reflects ongoing efforts to ensure compliance with road safety regulations.

Following this operation, local residents may see increased police presence and enforcement on the roads. The community is encouraged to adhere to traffic laws to ensure safety for all road users.

articles.content_html:
Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) has announced that the 114 bus route will not serve the Rochdale Road stop until further notice due to ongoing building works nearby.

This change has been in effect since October 20, and there is currently no specified date for when the stop will reopen.

In addition to the changes affecting route 114, the 38 bus route is on diversion during the evenings and overnight due to road closures on Chapel Street in Salford.

This diversion is scheduled to last from November 4 to November 7 and again from November 9 to November 11, affecting services between 7pm and 5am.

Passengers using the 114 route should be aware that the stop on Oldham Street is also temporarily out of service due to carriageway repairs, but this stop is expected to reopen on November 6.

TfGM advises passengers to check live service alerts for the latest updates on affected routes, particularly those boarding on Chapel Street, Oldham Street, or Rochdale Road.

These changes may impact local commuters and residents who rely on these bus services for travel. Passengers are encouraged to plan their journeys accordingly and allow extra time for travel during the diversion periods.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council awards contract for Empty Homes Leasing Programme
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to CAREPOINT HC LIMITED for the GM Empty Homes TA Leasing Programme, aimed at providing temporary accommodation for families.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to CAREPOINT HC LIMITED for the GM Empty Homes Temporary Accommodation (TA) Leasing Programme. This framework contract is set for an initial term of four years or until the contract value reaches £3.5 million, whichever comes first.

The programme aims to lease or acquire 2-4 bedroom homes to provide temporary accommodation for families that the Council has a duty to support under sections 188, 190, or 193 of the Housing Act.

articles.title: New plans for Greggs bakery at Littleborough Service Station
articles.excerpt: Motor Fuel Group has submitted a planning application to Rochdale Council to establish a Greggs bakery at Littleborough Service Station, creating new jobs and utilising existing buildings.
articles.content_html:
Motor Fuel Group has submitted a planning application to Rochdale Council to establish a Greggs bakery at Littleborough Service Station on Church Street.

The proposal involves reconfiguring the existing jet-wash building to create a new shop with a single-storey front extension, while changing the use of the current shop to a retail bakery.

This new application follows a previous one submitted in October last year, which proposed demolishing the car-wash building to make way for a new bakery pod. However, that plan was withdrawn on June 30, as it was deemed unnecessary to demolish the existing structure.

The current proposal aims to make more efficient use of the existing buildings on site, retaining the established petrol filling station use.

If approved, the development is expected to create four full-time and four part-time jobs, contributing to local employment. JMS Planning, representing Motor Fuel Group, stated that the revised proposal is similar to the previous one but focuses on utilising existing facilities rather than demolition.

The application is currently under consideration by Rochdale Council, and local residents will be keen to see how this development could enhance the service station's offerings and potentially improve convenience for customers.

articles.title: Is there really a secret tunnel under Middleton between the Ring O’Bells and St Leonard’s?
articles.excerpt: Local tradition says a Civil War escape-passage ran from the Ring O’Bells’ cellars to Middleton Parish Church; documentary and heritage records find the legend persistent but not proved.
articles.summary: Local tradition says a Civil War escape-passage ran from the Ring O’Bells’ cellars to Middleton Parish Church; documentary and heritage records find the legend persistent but not proved.
articles.body:
Short answer: no verifiable evidence has been published that a continuous, built “secret tunnel” links the Ring O’Bells (the pub on St Leonard’s Square) and St Leonard’s Parish Church. What you can find are a long-lived local tradition, repeated accounts of Civil War‑era finds beneath the pub’s cellar, and a striking absence of confirmation in the formal heritage record.

The essentials are straightforward and local. St Leonard’s (the parish church on New Lane) is a Grade I listed building with medieval and post‑medieval fabric; its National Heritage List entry (List Entry No. 1162332) records the church’s architectural and historic interest (the entry was first listed on 15 March 1957). The Ring O’Bells stands opposite the church in Middleton town centre and is widely described in local guides as among the older buildings around the square. Those two facts — an ancient church on a hilltop and an old inn across the way — are what make the tunnel story so durable. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

What the legend says. articles.title: The Baum Rabbit: the ghostly white hare that belonged to St Mary in the Baum
articles.excerpt: A local boggart in the shape of a white rabbit was a fixture of Rochdale folklore around St Mary in the Baum; nineteenth‑century guides and dialect collections record how families used the story as a warning and a joke.
articles.summary: A local boggart in the shape of a white rabbit was a fixture of Rochdale folklore around St Mary in the Baum; nineteenth‑century guides and dialect collections record how families used the story as a warning and a joke.
articles.body:
You can still stand outside St Mary in the Baum on St Mary’s Gate and see how easy it would have been, in the years before the town filled the fields, to imagine something uncanny stirring among the tombstones. The church on this site was founded as a chapel of ease in the 1740s; today’s building dates to 1909–11. Local history collections record that the graveyard and its approaches were long the stage for a phantom known in the Lancashire dialect as the Baum Rabbit (or Baum Rappit). That, at least, is what the nineteenth‑century parish histories and later compilers say. (Facts about the church’s foundation and listing come from Historic England and the National Churches Trust; the folkloric note is recorded in local parish history.)

The simplest, best‑documented point is this: “Baum Rabbit” was a local name for a ghost story said to haunt the vicinity of St Mary’s Chapel (Cheetham Street). The entry in a standard history of the parish plainly describes the name and the traditional belief that a white rabbit haunted the chapel yard. That is a recorded piece of local tradition, not proof of anything supernatural. The primary value of the story is cultural: it shows what people around Rochdale saw, said and passed on about the town’s edges. (The parish history that records the entry is available in the local historical compilation.)

What do we know about how people used the tale? Nineteenth‑century and later printed sources and dialect collections suggest the Baum Rabbit behaved like other British “bogies” — a cautionary figure. Writers who collected local anecdotes and dialects quote the rabbit in short exchanges and refer to it as a thing to frighten children or explain odd noises. Folklorists and local historians have shown the phrase “baum‑rappit” used in speech as a shorthand reaction to something unlikely or imagined. In other words, for many Rochdale families the Baum Rabbit was a piece of verbal culture: a nursery bogey, a joking local mascot in dialect tales and an item of town gossip recorded in journals and collections.

How early is the story on the record? The church was established in the 1740s and the graveyard was part of a densely inhabited area by the mid‑nineteenth century; the Baum Rabbit appears in nineteenth‑century parish and dialect material and in local journals and sketches from that period. Later folklorists and a modern survey of local traditions have gathered those nineteenth‑century mentions into a recognisable thread. There is no reliable documentary evidence that the story is medieval; the available scholarship treats the rabbit as an eighteenth‑/nineteenth‑century urban graveyard boggart rather than an ancient relic.

Which details are uncertain or unverified? Several colourful claims turn up in later retellings — that the beast grew to enormous size, that it was shot and the shot passed through its body, or that clergy recorded sightings in parish registers. Those claims appear in popular retellings and should be treated cautiously; the surviving primary texts (parish history, dialect entries and contemporary newspapers cited in later studies) do not substantiate sensational particulars. Where a specific newspaper or diary entry names a date or witness, scholars either quote it precisely or mark it as anecdote; where no such original is found, the safer judgment is that the detail is part of oral amplification.

Why did Rochdale keep telling the story? The Baum Rabbit seems to have worked on several levels: as a practical warning (keep children from the graveyard at night), as a local joke in dialect that marked belonging and identity, and as material for the town’s storytellers and periodicals. As urban Roche‑dale replaced fields and closed off some old shortcuts in the later nineteenth century, those physical changes also altered the story’s stage; yet the name survives in local memory and even in pub names and tourist notes.

If you’re after a next step: the best primary places to follow the trail are the parish history entries that note the Baum Rabbit and the official record on the church’s history and listing. Those give you the verifiable facts — where the chapel stood, when the present building dates from and that a ghostly rabbit was part of local tradition — and let you read the folklore in its proper, human context.

articles.title: Did goblins move Rochdale Parish Church up the hill?
articles.excerpt: A long-told local tale says unseen workers carried building stones overnight to the top of the hill; the record shows a medieval church, later Victorian work, and a 19th‑century storyteller rather than supernatural masons.
articles.summary: A long-told local tale says unseen workers carried building stones overnight to the top of the hill; the record shows a medieval church, later Victorian work, and a 19th‑century storyteller rather than supernatural masons.
articles.body:
The short answer is: no, there is no evidence that goblins or other supernatural creatures physically moved the stones of St Chad’s Church. That story belongs to Lancashire folklore, best known from the 19th‑century collector John Roby, while the documentary and architectural record shows a long‑standing church site with medieval fabric and later restorations. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

Roby’s version of the tale — titled “The Goblin Builders” in his Traditions of Lancashire — describes a Saxon thane, piles of building stone laid by the river, and those materials mysteriously transferred overnight to the hill where St Chad’s now stands; Roby also notes the famous flight of steps (he records 124) leading up to the church. That account is a clear piece of local storytelling rather than a contemporary record of building work. Roby wrote in the 19th century as a folklorist and compiler of oral tradition; his retelling preserves how people in his era understood the place, not the legal or archaeological history of its masoning. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

The documented history of the building is plain and far less sensational. Historic England lists St Chad’s as Grade II* and describes medieval and post‑medieval construction phases: a thirteenth‑century tower, fourteenth‑century arcade columns and arches, a clerestory dated 1557, and substantial Victorian restorations and additions in the 19th century. Those layers — Norman and medieval masonry altered, repaired and refashioned over centuries — explain the church’s position and appearance more plausibly than an overnight relocation by invisible hands. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1045812))

Why on the hill? Practical and symbolic reasons usually guided medieval siting. A high position overlooks the river and the town, keeps the building clear of floodplain, and gives the church civic and visual prominence; these are the kinds of factors architectural historians use when they discuss hilltop parish churches, and they match the description of St Chad’s occupying high ground above the River Roch. The building’s long use as the mother church of the ancient parish of Rochdale — serving a large rural parish for many centuries — also favoured a prominent site. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1045812))

That is not to say the legend has no local value. Roby’s telling and other versions preserve a communal memory that the church’s siting felt important enough to explain with a story; the goblin motif is widespread in English folklore as a way to name unexplained or surprising events. Local guides and walking routes still point out the steps and repeat the tale; it’s part of how Rochdale people have talked about their church across generations. But folklore and documentary history are different tools: the former explains meaning, the latter records evidence. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

If you want to check the facts in person: the parish continues to use St Chad’s as Rochdale Parish Church, and the building, its steps and the churchyard are publicly accessible; the parish’s information pages list services and contact details. For the architectural inventory, Historic England’s official list entry gives the formal description and dating used by planners and conservators. If any reader is curious about the Roby story itself, his Traditions of Lancashire is available in full online as a 19th‑century account of local legend. ([rochdalecommunity.org.uk](https://rochdalecommunity.org.uk/sites/saint-chad-rochdale-parish-church/))

articles.title: Does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall?
articles.excerpt: Clegg Hall’s stone house and its Grade II* listing are facts; the boggart is a long‑lived story with no contemporary record to prove the medieval murder it’s said to haunt.
articles.summary: Clegg Hall’s stone house and its Grade II* listing are facts; the boggart is a long‑lived story with no contemporary record to prove the medieval murder it’s said to haunt.
articles.body:
Short answer: the house at Clegg Hall is real; the boggart belongs to folklore.

Clegg Hall stands on Clegg Hall Road, near Smithy Bridge (Milnrow) about two miles north‑east of Rochdale. The building you can see today is a protected, Grade II* listed house whose main fabric dates to about 1610; Historic England records that listing (List Entry 1309615, first listed 10 August 1951) and gives the architectural description and location. Those are verifiable, recent and public facts. The “boggart” stories are an older, oral and literary tradition layered over that solid record. 

What the documents say: local and county histories trace the place-name and family back to the medieval era but do not confirm the grisly crime the legend describes. Victorian county compilers and parish historians — the sources relied on by Historic England — record that the medieval Clegg family held land here, but that their holding had changed hands by the late 1200s and that later documentary evidence for a family murder is absent. In short: there is no surviving contemporary legal or parish record that corroborates the tale of an uncle murdering heirs by throwing them into a moat. (These points are set out in the local histories cited in the Historic England listing and in the History of the Parish of Rochdale.)

What the storytellers say: the best‑known version of the boggart appears in 19th‑century folklore collections. John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and other collectors printed lively accounts of a “Clegg‑Hall Boggart” — a malign household spirit variously called “Noman” in retellings — and filled them with theatrical incidents: a boggart chamber, a conjuring scene that includes the mock‑baptism of a fowl, and a supposed murderous plot to seize an inheritance. These tellings are valuable as folklore — they show how local people and writers shaped place and memory — but they are literary and oral sources written long after the events they describe. They do not stand in for primary legal evidence.

How historians and archivists treat the story: county historians and the Victoria County History tradition treat the Roby‑style tales as imaginative reconstructions rather than archival reportage. That judgement matters: antiquarian and folkloric writers of the 18th and 19th centuries enthusiastically collected local stories, but they also embroidered and adapted them for drama and moral lesson. Where a claim concerns a violent death or other serious matter, historians look for surviving deeds, court rolls, wills or parish registers. For Clegg Hall, those contemporary anchors for the boggart narrative are missing in the published local record.

Does anybody claim to have recent proof of a haunting? No. There is no official inspection, police finding, archaeological report or archival discovery published in primary sources that confirms the supernatural elements of the Clegg Hall tales. The house remains private property and its architectural listing is the public record that governs what the council and the public can rely on. If anyone hopes for an authoritative update (for example a newly found medieval deed or a published archaeological survey), that would need to appear in named archival catalogues, a local authority report or a recognised academic publication before it could alter the basic separation between folklore and documented history.

What readers can do and where to look next: if you want the verifiable facts about the building and its legal status, start with Historic England’s National Heritage List entry (List Entry 1309615). For the folklore side, read the contemporary printed collections such as John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and the 19th‑century county histories (often available in digitised form). If you want archival confirmation one way or another, Rochdale local studies and archives and the county record offices hold the primary material historians would consult; ask them for searches of deeds, manorial records and parish registers for Clegg/Clegg Hall — but be clear: until such primary documents are published or cited, the boggart remains a durable piece of local storytelling rather than a documented historical fact.

Verdict for the reader: Clegg Hall’s building and location are verifiable; its boggart lives in the region’s printed and oral folklore. That’s not the same as proof of a haunting or of a medieval murder supported by contemporary records. articles.content_html:
Short answer: the house at Clegg Hall is real; the boggart belongs to folklore.

Clegg Hall stands on Clegg Hall Road, near Smithy Bridge (Milnrow) about two miles north‑east of Rochdale.

The building you can see today is a protected, Grade II* listed house whose main fabric dates to about 1610; Historic England records that listing (List Entry 1309615, first listed 10 August 1951) and gives the architectural description and location.

Those are verifiable, recent and public facts. The “boggart” stories are an older, oral and literary tradition layered over that solid record.

What the documents say: local and county histories trace the place-name and family back to the medieval era but do not confirm the grisly crime the legend describes.

Victorian county compilers and parish historians — the sources relied on by Historic England — record that the medieval Clegg family held land here, but that their holding had changed hands by the late 1200s and that later documentary evidence for a family murder is absent.

In short: there is no surviving contemporary legal or parish record that corroborates the tale of an uncle murdering heirs by throwing them into a moat.

(These points are set out in the local histories cited in the Historic England listing and in the History of the Parish of Rochdale.)

What the storytellers say: the best‑known version of the boggart appears in 19th‑century folklore collections.

John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and other collectors printed lively accounts of a “Clegg‑Hall Boggart” — a malign household spirit variously called “Noman” in retellings — and filled them with theatrical incidents: a boggart chamber, a conjuring scene that includes the mock‑baptism of a fowl, and a supposed murderous plot to seize an inheritance.

These tellings are valuable as folklore — they show how local people and writers shaped place and memory — but they are literary and oral sources written long after the events they describe. They do not stand in for primary legal evidence.

How historians and archivists treat the story: county historians and the Victoria County History tradition treat the Roby‑style tales as imaginative reconstructions rather than archival reportage.

That judgement matters: antiquarian and folkloric writers of the 18th and 19th centuries enthusiastically collected local stories, but they also embroidered and adapted them for drama and moral lesson.

Where a claim concerns a violent death or other serious matter, historians look for surviving deeds, court rolls, wills or parish registers. For Clegg Hall, those contemporary anchors for the boggart narrative are missing in the published local record.

Does anybody claim to have recent proof of a haunting? No. There is no official inspection, police finding, archaeological report or archival discovery published in primary sources that confirms the supernatural elements of the Clegg Hall tales.

The house remains private property and its architectural listing is the public record that governs what the council and the public can rely on.

If anyone hopes for an authoritative update (for example a newly found medieval deed or a published archaeological survey), that would need to appear in named archival catalogues, a local authority report or a recognised academic publication before it could alter the basic separation between folklore and documented history.

What readers can do and where to look next: if you want the verifiable facts about the building and its legal status, start with Historic England’s National Heritage List entry (List Entry 1309615).

For the folklore side, read the contemporary printed collections such as John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and the 19th‑century county histories (often available in digitised form).

If you want archival confirmation one way or another, Rochdale local studies and archives and the county record offices hold the primary material historians would consult; ask them for searches of deeds, manorial records and parish registers for Clegg/Clegg Hall — but be clear: until such primary documents are published or cited, the boggart remains a durable piece of local storytelling rather than a documented historical fact.

Verdict for the reader: Clegg Hall’s building and location are verifiable; its boggart lives in the region’s printed and oral folklore. That’s not the same as proof of a haunting or of a medieval murder supported by contemporary records.

For now, the boggart is a good story worth retelling — and a reminder to treat nineteenth‑century folklore as a literary and cultural source, not a court roll.
